newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Communist head to review euro position.
newsitem.headline: French Communist head to review euro position.

text.p: The leader of the French Communist party said on Monday that the party would review its position on the euro and he was reassured by recent statements on the stability pact by Prime Minister Lionel Jospin and finance minister Emmanuel Strauss-Kahn.

"We are in a period where we have to reposition ourselves in view of the fact we are in government," Robert Hue told a news conference when asked about his party's call for a referendum on the single European currency.
"We have to review our position on a whole series of questions. That is one of them," he said.
The Communist party gathered 700,000 signatures calling for a referendum on the euro, but it has not referred to the petition in recent weeks.
Hue said he found recent comments by Jospin and Strauss-Kahn's position on the stability pact encouraging.
"I note that a certain number of things written by the prime minister and the economy and finance minister today on the stability pact go along with the direction of left organisations," he said.

Strauss-Kahn said at a meeting of European Union finance ministers in Luxembourg that France would need more than a week to consider the stability pact, which France wants to be amended with an attachment on employment.

"I am glad that Lionel Jospin has said that he will keep at the European level the commitments made during the election campaign -- those of the joint declaration (of the Socialist and Communist parties), particularly those which say that we cannot go for an austerity policy...that we have to have a different European policy, " Hue said.
Hue's news conference was part of a series of "citiziens' meetings" due to be held throughout France.

French officials in Luxembourg said Strauss-Kahn had said the new government wanted to discuss the stability pact with the National Assembly and could not do so until June 19, two days after the Amsterdam EU summit.
The stability pact is aimed at keeping public deficits down after the launch of the euro in 1999 and would fine states which ran excessive deficits.
